claim: Between March 2020 and November 2020, 451 healthcare workers, patients, and patient contacts at participating North London Hospitals were diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2 by PCR.
source: Between March 2020 and November 2020, 451 healthcare workers, patients, and patient contacts at the participating North London Hospitals were diagnosed at the Camelia Botnar Laboratories with SARS-CoV-2 by PCR as part of a routine staff diagnostic service at Great Ormond Street Hospital NHS Foundation Trust (GOSH).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers and dates from the study cohort.

claim: A total of 289 isolates were whole-genome sequenced using the Illumina NextSeq platform, resulting in 522 whole-genome sequences including longitudinal and technical replicates.
source: A total of 289 isolates were whole-genome sequenced using the Illumina NextSeq platform, which resulted in 522 whole-genome sequences including longitudinal and technical replicates (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific sequencing data from the study.

claim: The mean participant age was 40 years.
source: The mean participant age was 40 years of age (median 38.5 years of age, interquartile range [IQR] 30–50 years of age), and 60% of the participants were female (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides demographic statistics from the study cohort.

claim: 60% of the participants were female.
source: The mean participant age was 40 years of age (median 38.5 years of age, interquartile range [IQR] 30–50 years of age), and 60% of the participants were female (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides demographic statistics from the study cohort.

claim: All samples were SARS-CoV-2 positive with real-time qPCR cycle threshold (Ct) values ranging from 16 to 35 cycles.
source: All samples were SARS-CoV-2 positive with real-time qPCR cycle threshold (Ct) values ranging from 16 to 35 cycles (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the range of Ct values from PCR testing.

claim: The earliest sample was collected on March 26, 2020.
source: The earliest sample was collected on March 26, 2020, while the latest one dated to November 4, 2020 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific dates for sample collection and references a figure.

claim: The latest sample was collected on November 4, 2020.
source: The earliest sample was collected on March 26, 2020, while the latest one dated to November 4, 2020 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific dates for sample collection and references a figure.

claim: The mean time from symptom onset to sample collection date was 5 days for samples with self-reported symptom onset data.
source: A total of 291 samples had self-reported symptom onset data, for which the mean time from symptom onset to sample collection date was 5 days (IQR 2–7 days, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The manuscript reports timing statistics from the study cohort.

claim: More than 90% of the samples were taken from hospital staff.
source: More than 90% of the samples were taken from hospital staff, while the rest comprised patients and contacts of either the patients or the staff members (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides the composition of the study cohort.

claim: A total of 454 whole genomes with mean coverage higher than 10× were kept for further analysis.
source: A total of 454 whole genomes with mean coverage higher than 10× were kept for further analysis, resulting in an average coverage across isolates of 2457× (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports sequencing quality metrics.

claim: The average coverage across isolates was 2457×.
source: A total of 454 whole genomes with mean coverage higher than 10× were kept for further analysis, resulting in an average coverage across isolates of 2457× (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports sequencing quality metrics.

claim: Allele frequencies were extracted using the pileup functionality within bcftools with a minimum base and mapping quality of 30.
source: Allele frequencies were extracted using the pileup functionality within bcftools (Danecek et al., 2011) with a minimum base and mapping quality of 30, which represents a base call error rate of 0.1%.
evidence: The manuscript describes the bioinformatics methods used.

claim: A minimum base and mapping quality of 30 represents a base call error rate of 0.1%.
source: Allele frequencies were extracted using the pileup functionality within bcftools (Danecek et al., 2011) with a minimum base and mapping quality of 30, which represents a base call error rate of 0.1%.
evidence: The manuscript provides the interpretation of quality scores.

claim: Only minor variants with an allele frequency of at least 2% were kept as putative variants.
source: Only minor variants with an allele frequency of at least 2% were kept as putative variants.
evidence: The manuscript describes the filtering criteria used.

claim: Samples with a frequency of missing bases higher than 10% were excluded, keeping 350 isolates for analysis.
source: Samples with a frequency of missing bases higher than 10% were excluded, keeping 350 isolates for analysis.
evidence: The manuscript describes the filtering criteria and resulting sample size.

claim: The mean number of low-frequency variants was 12.
source: The mean number of low-frequency variants was 12 (median 3, IQR 1.00–9.75), although both the number of variants and its deviation increased at high Ct values (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistics on within-host variation.

claim: The number of variants and its deviation increased at high Ct values.
source: The mean number of low-frequency variants was 12 (median 3, IQR 1.00–9.75), although both the number of variants and its deviation increased at high Ct values (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports an observed relationship between Ct values and variant numbers.

claim: Technical replicates of 17 samples were sequenced and analyzed.
source: To understand the stability of within-sample variation and minimize spurious variant calls, we sequenced and analyzed technical replicates of 17 samples.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design.

claim: When the variant was present in both duplicates, the correlation of the variant frequencies was high (R2=0.9).
source: Overall, when the variant was present in both duplicates the correlation of the variant frequencies was high (R2=0.9, Figure 1a, right).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical measure of correlation between technical replicates.

claim: The high correlation was maintained at low variant frequencies.
source: The high correlation was also maintained at low variant frequencies (Figure 1a, left).
evidence: The manuscript reports consistency of correlation across frequency ranges.

claim: Minor variants were less likely to be shared when one or more of the paired samples had low viral load.
source: Minor variants were less likely to be shared when one or more of the paired samples had low viral load.
evidence: The manuscript reports an observed relationship between viral load and variant sharing.

claim: The mean proportion of discrepant within-sample variants between duplicated samples was 0.39.
source: The mean proportion of discrepant within-sample variants between duplicated samples was 0.39 (sd = 0.29), although this varied between duplicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical measure of discrepancy between replicates.

claim: Ct values in RT-PCR obtained during viral amplification are inversely correlated with viral load.
source: Ct values in RT-PCR obtained during viral amplification are inversely correlated with viral load (Tom and Mina, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this relationship.

claim: The proportion of shared intra-host variants was negatively correlated with Ct values in a logistic model (estimate = −0.78, p-value = 0.008).
source: The proportion of shared intra-host variants was negatively correlated with Ct values in a logistic model (estimate = −0.78, p-value = 0.008), with higher Ct values associated with a lower amount of shared intra-host variants (Figure 1c).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from statistical modeling.

claim: Higher Ct values were associated with a lower amount of shared intra-host variants.
source: The proportion of shared intra-host variants was negatively correlated with Ct values in a logistic model (estimate = −0.78, p-value = 0.008), with higher Ct values associated with a lower amount of shared intra-host variants (Figure 1c).
evidence: The manuscript reports an observed relationship from statistical analysis.

claim: The number of within-sample variants detected increased with Ct value.
source: The number of within-sample variants detected also increased with Ct value, as well as the deviation in the number of variants between duplicates (Figure 1d).
evidence: The manuscript reports an observed relationship between Ct values and variant numbers.

claim: The deviation in the number of variants between duplicates increased with Ct value.
source: The number of within-sample variants detected also increased with Ct value, as well as the deviation in the number of variants between duplicates (Figure 1d).
evidence: The manuscript reports an observed relationship between Ct values and variant variability.

claim: The increase in within-sample variants at high Ct values could be explained by an increase in spurious variants at low viral loads.
source: This could be explained either by an increase in the number of spurious variants at low viral loads (Tonkin-Hill et al., 2021), biased amplification of low-level subpopulations minor rare alleles (McCrone and Lauring, 2016), or due to the accumulation of within-host variation through time, as late stages of infection are usually characterized by high Ct values (low viral load).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this potential explanation.

claim: The increase in within-sample variants at high Ct values could be explained by biased amplification of low-level subpopulations.
source: This could be explained either by an increase in the number of spurious variants at low viral loads (Tonkin-Hill et al., 2021), biased amplification of low-level subpopulations minor rare alleles (McCrone and Lauring, 2016), or due to the accumulation of within-host variation through time, as late stages of infection are usually characterized by high Ct values (low viral load).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this potential explanation.

claim: The increase in within-sample variants at high Ct values could be explained by the accumulation of within-host variation through time.
source: This could be explained either by an increase in the number of spurious variants at low viral loads (Tonkin-Hill et al., 2021), biased amplification of low-level subpopulations minor rare alleles (McCrone and Lauring, 2016), or due to the accumulation of within-host variation through time, as late stages of infection are usually characterized by high Ct values (low viral load).
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning based on infection dynamics.

claim: Late stages of infection are usually characterized by high Ct values (low viral load).
source: This could be explained either by an increase in the number of spurious variants at low viral loads (Tonkin-Hill et al., 2021), biased amplification of low-level subpopulations minor rare alleles (McCrone and Lauring, 2016), or due to the accumulation of within-host variation through time, as late stages of infection are usually characterized by high Ct values (low viral load).
evidence: The manuscript states a general characteristic of infection progression.

claim: Only samples with a Ct value equal or lower than 30 cycles were considered for analysis.
source: Based on these results, only samples with a Ct value equal or lower than 30 cycles were considered, which resulted in 249 samples kept for analysis.
evidence: The manuscript describes the filtering criteria applied.

claim: 249 samples were kept for analysis after filtering by Ct value.
source: Based on these results, only samples with a Ct value equal or lower than 30 cycles were considered, which resulted in 249 samples kept for analysis.
evidence: The manuscript reports the resulting sample size after filtering.

claim: Only variants with a frequency higher or equal than 2% were used.
source: Additionally, only variants with a frequency higher or equal than 2% were used.
evidence: The manuscript describes the filtering criteria applied.

claim: 414 out of 29,903 positions were polymorphic for the consensus sequence.
source: For the filtered dataset, 414 out of 29,903 positions were polymorphic for the consensus sequence, while the alignment with within-sample diversity had 1039 SNPs.
evidence: The manuscript reports genomic variation statistics.

claim: The alignment with within-sample diversity had 1039 SNPs.
source: For the filtered dataset, 414 out of 29,903 positions were polymorphic for the consensus sequence, while the alignment with within-sample diversity had 1039 SNPs.
evidence: The manuscript reports genomic variation statistics.

claim: 699 positions had intra-host diversity.
source: Of these, 699 positions had intra-host diversity, of which 78% (549/699) were singletons.
evidence: The manuscript reports genomic variation statistics.

claim: 78% of positions with intra-host diversity were singletons.
source: Of these, 699 positions had intra-host diversity, of which 78% (549/699) were singletons.
evidence: The manuscript reports genomic variation statistics.

claim: 83% of samples contained at least one position with a high-quality within-host variant.
source: The majority of samples (207/249, 83%) contained at least one position with a high-quality within-host variant, and the median amount of intra-host variants per sample was 2 (IQR 1–4.5).
evidence: The manuscript reports the prevalence of within-host variation.

claim: The median amount of intra-host variants per sample was 2.
source: The majority of samples (207/249, 83%) contained at least one position with a high-quality within-host variant, and the median amount of intra-host variants per sample was 2 (IQR 1–4.5).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistics on within-host variation.

claim: Epidemiological data is often necessary to infer the directionality of transmission given the limited genomic information in consensus sequences.
source: Given the limited genomic information in the consensus sequences, epidemiological data is often necessary to infer the directionality of transmission.
evidence: The manuscript states a limitation of consensus sequence approaches.

claim: Pairs of samples from the same hospital, department, epidemiologically linked, or longitudinal and technical replicates had a lower SNP distance than those samples that did not have any relationship.
source: Pairs of samples from the same hospital, department, epidemiologically linked, or longitudinal and technical replicates had a lower SNP distance (were more closely related) than those samples that did not have any relationship, although this difference was small in the case of pairs of samples from the same hospital (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from statistical analysis comparing SNP distances.

claim: The difference in SNP distance was small for pairs of samples from the same hospital.
source: Pairs of samples from the same hospital, department, epidemiologically linked, or longitudinal and technical replicates had a lower SNP distance (were more closely related) than those samples that did not have any relationship, although this difference was small in the case of pairs of samples from the same hospital (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports a specific observation about hospital-level relationships.

claim: The proportion of shared within-host variants was higher between technical replicates, longitudinal duplicates, epidemiologically linked samples, and samples from the same department compared to pairs with no epidemiological links.
source: The proportion of shared within-host variants was higher between technical replicates, longitudinal duplicates, epidemiologically linked samples, and samples taken from individuals from the same department when compared to pairs with no epidemiological links, although the range of this probability was large (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from analysis of variant sharing.

claim: The range of the probability of sharing within-host variants was large.
source: The proportion of shared within-host variants was higher between technical replicates, longitudinal duplicates, epidemiologically linked samples, and samples taken from individuals from the same department when compared to pairs with no epidemiological links, although the range of this probability was large (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports variability in the observed relationship.

claim: The probability of sharing a low-frequency variant tended to increase with variant frequency, but the association was not strong (odds ratio 1.8, 95% CI 0.9–3.5, p=0.08).
source: There was a tendency for the probability to increase with variant frequency, but the association was not strong (odds ratio 1.8, 95% CI 0.9–3.5, p=0.08).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from logistic regression modeling.

claim: Pairs from the same department, with epidemiological links, replicates, or technical replicates all had a significantly higher probability of sharing a low-frequency variant compared to pairs with no link (all Wald test p-values <0.001).
source: On the other hand, pairs from the same department, with epidemiological links, replicates, or technical replicates all had a significantly higher probability of sharing a low-frequency variant when compared to those pairs with no link (all Wald test p-values <0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from statistical testing.

claim: The inferred probability of sharing low-frequency variants for pairs from the same department was 1.4% (95% CI 0.9–2.1%).
source: The inferred probabilities for pairs from the sample department was 1.4% (95% CI 0.9–2.1%), which increased to 5% for pairs with epidemiological links (95% CI 4.2–6.4%).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from logistic regression modeling.

claim: The inferred probability of sharing low-frequency variants for pairs with epidemiological links was 5% (95% CI 4.2–6.4%).
source: The inferred probabilities for pairs from the sample department was 1.4% (95% CI 0.9–2.1%), which increased to 5% for pairs with epidemiological links (95% CI 4.2–6.4%).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from logistic regression modeling.

claim: For longitudinal replicates, the probability of sharing low-frequency variants was 38% (95% CI 35–41%).
source: For longitudinal replicates, the probability was inferred to be 38% (95% CI 35–41%), and were shared between multiple time points (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from logistic regression modeling.

claim: Low-frequency variants were shared between multiple time points in longitudinal replicates.
source: For longitudinal replicates, the probability was inferred to be 38% (95% CI 35–41%), and were shared between multiple time points (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from longitudinal data and references a figure.

claim: Technical replicates had the highest probability of sharing low-frequency variants at 70% (95% CI 64–76%).
source: Technical replicates were estimated to have the highest probability (70%, 95% CI 64–76%).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from logistic regression modeling.

claim: 100 random phylogenetic trees with 100 tips each were generated for simulation testing.
source: To test the accuracy of different models at inferring known phylogenies, 100 random phylogenetic trees with 100 tips each were generated using the function rtree within the R package ape (Paradis et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript describes the simulation methodology.

claim: Whole-genome alignments were simulated from the random phylogenies using a model with 16-character states representing combinations of nucleotides as minor and major alleles.
source: Whole-genome alignments were simulated from the random 100 phylogenies with the function SimSeq of the R package phangorn (R Development Core Team, 2021; Schliep, 2011) using a model with 16-character states that represent the combinations of the four nucleotides with each other as minor and major alleles (Figure 3d).
evidence: The manuscript describes the simulation methodology.

claim: In the simulation model, fixed bases (A, C, G, and T) were 100 times more frequent than low-frequency bases.
source: This rates result in fixed bases (A, C, G, and T) being 100 times more frequent than low-frequency bases.
evidence: The manuscript describes the parameters used in simulations.

claim: For all metrics employed, phylogenies inferred using within-host diversity approximated better to the initial tree than those using consensus sequences.
source: For all the metrics employed, the phylogenies inferred explicitly using within-host diversity as independent characters approximated better to the initial tree than the one using the consensus sequence (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from simulation comparisons.

claim: The transition/transversion rates inferred by phylogenetic models accounting for within-host diversity accurately reflect the rates used for the simulation of genomic sequences.
source: Additionally, the transition/transversion rates inferred by the phylogenetic models accounting for within-host diversity accurately reflect the rates used for the simulation of genomic sequences (Supplementary files 4–6).
evidence: The manuscript reports validation of the model parameters.

claim: Using rates that promote abundant and stable low-frequency variation made the 16-state model perform better than the consensus sequence model.
source: As expected, choosing rates that promote an abundant and stable landscape of low-frequency variation (rate of minor variant acquisition of 20, and rates of variant switch and lost of 1) made the 16-state model to perform better than the model using consensus sequences, which improved as the proportion of low-frequency variants decreased (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from simulations with varying parameters.

claim: In simulations using a Jukes-Cantor DNA model without low-frequency variation, both models showed similar results.
source: Conversely, in simulations using a Jukes-Cantor DNA model, and therefore without any low-frequency variation, both models showed similar results (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from simulations without within-host variation.

claim: For all metrics used, the model using low-frequency variants inferred phylogenies more similar to the starting coalescent tree than those inferred using consensus sequences.
source: For all metrics used, the model using low-frequency variants inferred phylogenies more similar to the starting coalescent tree than those inferred using the consensus sequence (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from coalescent simulations.

claim: Outbreaks were simulated with a host population varying between 10 and 15 hosts.
source: We simulated outbreaks using TransPhylo (Didelot et al., 2017) with a host population varying between 10 and 15 hosts, no recombination, complete sampling of the outbreak, and selecting epidemiological parameters to match the transmission dynamics of SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: The manuscript describes the outbreak simulation parameters.

claim: Using consensus sequences performed better than a random distribution of trees in outbreak simulations.
source: Even though using consensus sequences performed better than a random distribution of trees, using within-host diversity outperformed the consensus sequence in all instances (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from outbreak simulations.

claim: Using within-host diversity outperformed consensus sequences in all outbreak simulation instances.
source: Even though using consensus sequences performed better than a random distribution of trees, using within-host diversity outperformed the consensus sequence in all instances (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from outbreak simulations.

claim: Phylogenies inferred using within-host diversity were more similar to the real outbreak phylogeny for wider bottleneck sizes.
source: The phylogenies inferred using within-host diversity were more similar to the real outbreak phylogeny for wider bottleneck sizes, with the best performance when no bottleneck was present.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from outbreak simulations with varying bottleneck sizes.

claim: Phylogenies inferred using within-host diversity showed best performance when no bottleneck was present.
source: The phylogenies inferred using within-host diversity were more similar to the real outbreak phylogeny for wider bottleneck sizes, with the best performance when no bottleneck was present.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from outbreak simulations.

claim: Genome sequences collected at different time points are expected to diverge as time progresses, resulting in a positive correlation between isolation date and accumulated mutations (temporal signal).
source: Genome sequences collected at different time points are expected to diverge as time progresses, resulting in a positive correlation between the isolation date and the number of accumulated mutations (temporal signal) (Rieux and Balloux, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this expectation.

claim: Longitudinal samples in the phylogeny inferred using within-host diversity showed an increase in genetic distance as time progressed (coefficient 2.24, 0.59–3.88 95% CI, p=0.019).
source: Longitudinal samples in the phylogeny inferred using within-host diversity reflected the expected temporal signal, with an increase in genetic distance as time progressed between the longitudinal pairs in a linear model (coefficient 2.24, 0.59–3.88 95% CI, p=0.019, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from linear modeling of temporal relationships.

claim: The difference in Ct value among longitudinal duplicates was not correlated with higher genetic distances (coefficient 1.62, –0.66 to 3.91 95% CI, p=0.2).
source: The difference in Ct value among longitudinal duplicates was not correlated with higher genetic distances (coefficient 1.62, –0.66 to 3.91 95% CI, p=0.2).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from statistical analysis.

claim: As outbreaks progressed, the number of low-frequency variants increased (coefficient 0.16, 0.06–0.27 95% CI, p=0.003, r2=0.19).
source: In general, as the outbreaks progressed the number of low-frequency variants increased (coefficient 0.16, 0.06–0.27 95% CI, p=0.003, r2=0.19, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from linear modeling of outbreak progression.

claim: The majority of clusters (10/11) with identical consensus sequences showed a positive correlation between distance to root and collection dates when using within-sample diversity.
source: The majority of clusters (10/11) showed a positive correlation between the distance of the tips to the root and the collection dates, demonstrating a significant temporal signal between samples when there was none using the conventional consensus tree (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from root-to-tip analysis.

claim: Clusters with identical consensus sequences demonstrated significant temporal signal when using within-sample diversity where there was none using conventional consensus trees.
source: The majority of clusters (10/11) showed a positive correlation between the distance of the tips to the root and the collection dates, demonstrating a significant temporal signal between samples when there was none using the conventional consensus tree (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript reports results comparing consensus and within-host diversity approaches.

claim: A time-calibrated phylogeny was inferred using BactDating with collection dates of the tips.
source: To illustrate the downstream application of the improved phylogenetic resolution, we inferred a time-calibrated phylogeny from the phylogeny inferred using the 16-character state model with the collection dates of the tips using BactDating (Didelot et al., 2018; Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and calculated the likelihood of transmission events within potential epidemiologically identified outbreaks using a susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed (SEIR) model (Lekone and Finkenstädt, 2006; Eldholm et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analysis methodology.

claim: The SEIR model was parameterized with an average latency period of 5.5 days.
source: The SEIR model was parameterized with an average latency period of 5.5 days (Xin et al., 2022), an infectious period of 6 days (Byrne et al., 2020), and a within-host coalescent rate of 5 days as previously estimated for SARS-CoV-2 (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites references for the parameter values used.

claim: The SEIR model was parameterized with an infectious period of 6 days.
source: The SEIR model was parameterized with an average latency period of 5.5 days (Xin et al., 2022), an infectious period of 6 days (Byrne et al., 2020), and a within-host coalescent rate of 5 days as previously estimated for SARS-CoV-2 (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites references for the parameter values used.

claim: The SEIR model was parameterized with a within-host coalescent rate of 5 days as previously estimated for SARS-CoV-2.
source: The SEIR model was parameterized with an average latency period of 5.5 days (Xin et al., 2022), an infectious period of 6 days (Byrne et al., 2020), and a within-host coalescent rate of 5 days as previously estimated for SARS-CoV-2 (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference for the parameter value used.

claim: Within-sample genetic diversity is common among a wide variety of pathogens.
source: Within-sample genetic diversity is common among a wide variety of pathogens (Mongkolrattanothai et al., 2011; Lieberman et al., 2016; Dinis et al., 2016; Leitner, 2019; Popa et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references to support this claim.

claim: Within-host diversity may be generated de novo during infection, by a single transmission event of a diverse inoculum, or by independent transmission events from multiple sources.
source: This diversity may be generated de novo during infection, by a single transmission event of a diverse inoculum or by independent transmission events from multiple sources (Worby et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support the mechanisms of diversity generation.

claim: The maintenance and dynamic of within-host diversity is a product of natural selection, genetic drift, and fluctuating population size.
source: The maintenance and dynamic of within-host diversity is then a product of natural selection, genetic drift, and fluctuating population size (Didelot et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this evolutionary principle.

claim: The transmission of within-host variation between individuals is favored as a large inoculum exposure is more likely to give rise to infection.
source: The transmission of within-host variation between individuals is also favored as a large inoculum exposure is more likely to give rise to infection (Murphy et al., 1984; Han et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2022; Sender et al., 2021; Spinelli et al., 2021; Trunfio et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references to support this claim.

claim: The amount of within-sample diversity transmitted from index case to contact is determined by the bottleneck size.
source: The amount of within-sample diversity transmitted from index case to contact is determined by the bottleneck size (Zwart and Elena, 2015), with stringent bottlenecks limiting the number of genotypes transmitted from the host to the recipient, and wide bottlenecks allowing for the transmission of higher levels of genetic diversity (Worby et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to support this relationship.

claim: Stringent bottlenecks limit the number of genotypes transmitted from the host to the recipient.
source: The amount of within-sample diversity transmitted from index case to contact is determined by the bottleneck size (Zwart and Elena, 2015), with stringent bottlenecks limiting the number of genotypes transmitted from the host to the recipient, and wide bottlenecks allowing for the transmission of higher levels of genetic diversity (Worby et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this mechanism.

claim: Wide bottlenecks allow for the transmission of higher levels of genetic diversity.
source: The amount of within-sample diversity transmitted from index case to contact is determined by the bottleneck size (Zwart and Elena, 2015), with stringent bottlenecks limiting the number of genotypes transmitted from the host to the recipient, and wide bottlenecks allowing for the transmission of higher levels of genetic diversity (Worby et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this mechanism.

claim: The substitution rate of SARS-CoV-2 has been inferred to be around two mutations per genome per month.
source: For instance, the substitution rate of SARS-CoV-2 has been inferred to be around two mutations per genome per month (Harvey et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference for this rate estimate.

claim: The infectious period of SARS-CoV-2 is 6 days.
source: Given its infectious period of 6 days (Byrne et al., 2020), most consensus sequences in a small-scale outbreak will show no variation between them.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference for this parameter.

claim: Most consensus sequences in a small-scale SARS-CoV-2 outbreak will show no variation between them.
source: Given its infectious period of 6 days (Byrne et al., 2020), most consensus sequences in a small-scale outbreak will show no variation between them.
evidence: The manuscript infers this consequence from the mutation rate and infectious period.

claim: Previous work has shown the advantages of using within-host diversity to infer transmission events compared to using consensus sequences.
source: Previous work has shown the advantages of using within-host diversity to infer transmission events compared to using consensus sequences (Wymant et al., 2018; De Maio et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites references to prior work.

claim: Including within-sample diversity in a phylogenetic model would significantly increase the evolutionary and temporal signal.
source: We hypothesize that the failure of consensus sequence approaches to capture within-sample variation arbitrarily excludes meaningful data and limits pathogen phylogenetic and transmission inference, and that including within-sample diversity in a phylogenetic model would significantly increase the evolutionary and temporal signal and thereby improve our ability to infer infectious disease phylogenies and transmission events.
evidence: This is the stated hypothesis of the study.

claim: The failure of consensus sequence approaches to capture within-sample variation arbitrarily excludes meaningful data and limits pathogen phylogenetic and transmission inference.
source: We hypothesize that the failure of consensus sequence approaches to capture within-sample variation arbitrarily excludes meaningful data and limits pathogen phylogenetic and transmission inference, and that including within-sample diversity in a phylogenetic model would significantly increase the evolutionary and temporal signal and thereby improve our ability to infer infectious disease phylogenies and transmission events.
evidence: This is part of the stated hypothesis of the study.

claim: Understanding who infects whom in an infectious disease outbreak is a key component of infection prevention and control.
source: Understanding who infects whom in an infectious disease outbreak is a key component of infection prevention and control (Didelot et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this statement.

claim: The limited genetic diversity of many pathogens often hinders understanding of transmission events.
source: The use of whole-genome sequencing allows for detailed investigation of disease outbreaks, but the limited genetic diversity of many pathogens often hinders our understanding of transmission events (Campbell et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference to support this limitation.

claim: Many index case and contact pairs will share identical genotypes, making it difficult to ascertain who infected whom.
source: As a consequence of the limited diversity, many index case and contact pairs will share identical genotypes, making it difficult to ascertain who infected whom.
evidence: The manuscript infers this consequence from limited diversity.

claim: Conventional whole-genome sequencing phylogenetic approaches exclusively use consensus sequences.
source: Although within-host genetic diversity is common among a wide variety of pathogens, conventional whole-genome sequencing phylogenetic approaches exclusively use consensus sequences, which consider only the most prevalent nucleotide at each position and therefore fail to capture low-frequency variation within samples.
evidence: The manuscript describes current standard practice.

claim: Consensus sequences consider only the most prevalent nucleotide at each position and fail to capture low-frequency variation within samples.
source: Although within-host genetic diversity is common among a wide variety of pathogens, conventional whole-genome sequencing phylogenetic approaches exclusively use consensus sequences, which consider only the most prevalent nucleotide at each position and therefore fail to capture low-frequency variation within samples.
